hypothesis: The nucleic acid adopts a double-helical architecture where two antiparallel polynucleotide chains are held together by specific hydrogen-bonding interactions between complementary base pairs, creating a uniform structural width that accommodates the helical geometry.
mechanism: The Rule establishes Chargaff's parity and diffraction data indicative of a regular helix; the Case posits that complementary base pairing (A-T and G-C) provides the chemical specificity for replication, while the double-stranded nature explains the helical pitch and axial spacing. This structure allows for semi-conservative replication because each strand serves as a template for the synthesis of a new complementary strand, preserving the base-pairing rule in daughter molecules.
observations_explained: The uniform diameter of the DNA helix is maintained regardless of sequence because purine-pyrimidine pairing ensures consistent width.
The stability of the double helix against thermal denaturation correlates with the number of hydrogen bonds and base stacking interactions.
parsimony_justification: This hypothesis avoids ad-hoc assumptions about separate replication machinery by deriving the copying mechanism directly from the structural complementarity of the molecule itself.
novelty_justification: It infers a specific tertiary structural arrangement (double helix with H-bonds) from secondary chemical data (base ratios) and physical measurements (diffraction), rather than merely describing the chemical composition.

candidate_survey.label: retrieval
candidate_survey.description: The Watson-Crick double helix model with specific base pairing.

candidate_survey.label: historical_decoy
candidate_survey.description: The polymeric chain model where bases are on the exterior, proposed by Pauling, which failed to explain Chargaff's rules and replication fidelity.

candidate_survey.label: abductive
candidate_survey.description: A double-stranded antiparallel helix where genetic information is encoded by the sequence of bases, and replication is driven by the thermodynamic preference for complementary base pairing.
